functionalObligations.text: a route is constructed across venues the user did not choose, and returned as a fully assembled transaction the user need only sign
the order is split across paths to a granularity of 0.01 percent by numerical optimisation (golden-section search and Brent's method) rather than by enumeration
functionalObligations.note: Ag covers route construction and therefore covers this, but it cannot distinguish a router that enumerates from one that optimises, nor record the 100x performance difference Jupiter attributes to the change. Recorded so the construction is not read as ignoring the engine.

functionalObligations.text: quotes are solicited from independent third-party routing protocols as well as from venues, and the winning quote may come from a rival aggregator rather than from a pool
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE, and the nesting finding this lane was asked to surface. Four engines compete inside one product: Metis/Iris and JupiterZ (Jupiter's own) against DFlow, OKX and Hashflow (other protocols'). Two of those leaves, OKX and DFlow, are separately ranked rows in this same corpus category. Ag names multi-venue route construction and has no composition operator, so it cannot express an Ag whose leaves are Ag. A flat ranking of this category double-counts volume and mis-attributes execution: a system that routes to routers is doing something a system that routes to venues is not.

functionalObligations.text: candidate routes are simulated on-chain before one is chosen, and are ranked on predicted executed price rather than on quoted price
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. A distinct epistemic act: the mechanism does not trust its own quotes and buys evidence before committing. Nothing in the 58 names simulate-before-choose, and Ag presumes the quote is the input to selection.

functionalObligations.text: quote sources that perform badly are automatically sidelined by the router without any governance act
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. The venue set is not a constant and is revised by the router's own measurement of its suppliers. No element names a self-adjusting supplier set; Aw would be a gate, and this is a performance ranking with no stated threshold (the rule is UNKNOWN).

functionalObligations.text: a market maker's price is accepted by a user-signed transaction that the maker then executes and pays the gas for, giving the taker zero slippage and no gas cost
functionalObligations.note: In IS REASSIGNED, not dropped. The corpus attaches In to Jupiter's limit/trigger/DCA products with a marker that the solver half is largely absent; under Trigger V2 those are custodial (see F14) and In fails there outright. It fits here instead: signed outcome constraints, a settlement verifier, competing third-party fillers, and a quote expiry with a fallback to on-chain routing, which is all four parts of L12. Gs is CANDIDATE-REGISTER and matches the corpus's own use at 1inch Fusion; L21's metering and fee settlement are absent.

functionalObligations.text: the market maker retains the right to decline execution after the taker has accepted its quote
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE, and a DEPARTURE FROM THE CORPUS: Rf is DROPPED from Jupiter's construction. Rf is defined as a signed maker quote and asserts firmness; a maker holding last look has sold an option, not a price. Jupiter's own API design concedes it, forbidding modification of an RFQ transaction and confining RFQ to the managed path for exactly this reason. Rf is therefore wrong in kind for JupiterZ rather than approximate, and the standing rule is that a finding of failure beats a forced fit. If stage 3 or the council prefers the forced fit, the alternative is Rf carried with a last-look marker; this lane's finding is failure.

functionalObligations.text: two mutually exclusive API paths exist with different guarantees: a managed path that assembles and lands the transaction, charges a platform fee and can use RFQ, and a raw-instruction path that is composable, carries no platform fee and can only use the in-house router
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE, the same dispatcher gap as OKX F9 in a different form. Here the caller chooses rather than the system, but the vocabulary equally cannot express that the fee, the composability and the set of available fill mechanisms all change with the choice.

functionalObligations.text: the signed transaction is submitted through infrastructure the protocol owns, a validator and RPC of its own, with a minimum tip, rather than through a public endpoint or a third-party relay
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. No symbol names the transaction's route to inclusion, and none names owning it. MEV protection here is not a service bought or a chain-level default inherited (contrast Binance Wallet F6) but a consequence of vertical integration into block production.

functionalObligations.text: the protocol publishes a measured average positive slippage of +0.63 basis points as a product property, that is, a claim that executed prices beat quoted prices
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. Price-improvement benchmarking stated as its own obligation per the stage-2 brief. The benchmark is the protocol's own quote and the measurement is the protocol's own, so it is unfalsifiable from outside; the corpus residue 'no element for route-quality guarantees / price-improvement sharing' is confirmed and sharpened into a published number.

functionalObligations.text: a platform fee is deducted inside the quote at a rate that depends on the asset classes being traded and rises to 50 basis points for any token listed within the previous 24 hours
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. Fd is the nearest and is rejected: Fd names the distribution of surplus and fees, not their levy, and nothing names a fee schedule conditioned on the age or class of the asset. Schedule is 0 bps for stable-to-stable, LST-to-LST and pairs into the protocol's own tokens, 2 bps SOL to stablecoin, 5 bps LST to stablecoin, 10 bps otherwise, 50 bps under 24 hours.

functionalObligations.text: the fee is collected in a priority-ordered choice among the pair's tokens rather than in a fixed leg
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. The protocol chooses which side of the trade to tax by the liquidity of the token (SOL, then stablecoins, then LSTs, then large caps, then other). No element names a fee whose denomination is itself a decision rule.

functionalObligations.text: an integrator sets a referral fee between 50 and 255 basis points on its users' trades and the protocol keeps 20 percent of it; if the integrator's fee account is uninitialised the trade still executes and the integrator simply gets nothing
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. A stated revenue split on someone else's users: distribution is sold, order flow is bought, and the price is a percentage of a fee neither party's user sees. This is the fourth distinct form the same unnameable primitive takes in this category (see LiquidMesh F10, OKX F11, KyberSwap F15).

functionalObligations.text: resting limit, OCO and recurring orders are held in a custodial vault operated by a third-party key manager, stored off-chain and private by default, rather than in an account the user controls
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE, and the largest single gap in this application. THE 58 CONTAIN NO SYMBOL FOR CUSTODY AT ALL, which is worth escalating beyond this category (Binance Wallet F9 is the same gap). In is rejected because In presumes a signed constraint any party can enforce at settlement, and here a custodian holds the funds. Ob is rejected because the order is not on-chain. Sb is rejected because the privacy is non-publication by a custodian, not shielded state with a nullifier set. Under V1 these orders were on-chain accounts; the change of custody is a change of category, not a detail, and the corpus predates it.

functionalObligations.text: a keeper operated by the protocol fires those orders when a US dollar price condition is met rather than a pool rate, sets the slippage for each slice itself, and the output amount is explicitly not guaranteed
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. Ex is rejected: the price is consumed off-chain by the protocol's own keeper and never verified on-chain, so there is no feed, no medianizer and no staleness bound to name. The corpus's rejection of the contested symbol Tw for scheduled execution is correct and is now stronger than the corpus knew, since the slices are keeper-fired from a custodial vault against a US dollar trigger, which is further from a TWAMM pool invariant than V1 was. No element names a scheduled or time-sliced execution, and none names an execution with no output guarantee.

functionalObligations.text: the protocol assigns tokens a quality score and a verification status of its own devising, which condition how a token is surfaced and what it costs to trade
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. A protocol-assigned quality label on the asset, feeding both display and price. LiquidMesh F16 is the same gap through a third-party risk vendor rather than an in-house score.

functionalObligations.text: access to the router is rationed by request-rate tier and filtered by country, IP range and request header, so who may ask the router for a price, and how often, is itself allocated
functionalObligations.note: APPROXIMATE, and a departure from the corpus {Ag, In, Rf}. Aw carries the deny rules; it cannot carry the graded rationing (0.5 to 150 requests per second), which is an allocation of execution quality rather than a binary permission. Used per this lane's standing principle: Aw for gates on the party seeking the service only.

functionalObligations.text: the routing engine is distributed as a closed binary and no source for the deployed aggregator program is published; a published audit inventory stands in its place
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. Two of this lane's five have converged on the same answer to how you distribute a router without publishing it (see OKX F16). Third-party claims that Jupiter is open source are not supported by the contents of the jup-ag organisation and are recorded here as resolved against the marketing claim. The compensating control is the audit set at https://developers.jup.ag/docs/resources/audits (accessed 2026-08-05), which no element expresses either.

functionalObligations.text: the router owns venues on the other side of its own routing: a perpetuals exchange, a lending market with flash loans, a liquid-staking token, a launchpad with bonding curves, a prediction market and a validator, so it can internalise the flow it receives
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. The corpus residue 'no element for the router also owning the venues it routes to' is confirmed and has grown since the corpus was written. Vertical order-flow capture has no symbol; note also that a construction listing Fl for Jupiter Lend would be capturing a different product, so Fl is deliberately not carried here.

functionalObligations.text: the protocol occupies four positions in the order-flow market at once: it owns the default trade surface on its chain, it buys routing from rival protocols, it sells the right to fill to market makers including the last-look privilege, and it sells distribution to integrators at a stated split
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE, and the central one. Order-flow ownership stated as its own obligation per the stage-2 brief. The party at category rank 6 whose explicit product is the sale of order flow (DFlow) sells into this system, so the buyer and the seller of order flow appear in the same corpus with no symbol distinguishing their positions.

paper.title: Jupiter
paper.label: cat:int:jupiter
paper.blurb: A meta-aggregator whose own documentation lists other routers --- including two members of this category --- as competitors inside its routing. It is not a peer of the others so much as a layer above some of them.
paper.witnessReason: The witness drops the quote element, because the venue's fills are subject to a last look and a quote that can be withdrawn at fill time is not the firm quote the element names. It reassigns the intent element from a component that has become custodial to the one that still answers to the definition.
paper.residueNote: That this venue routes to routers is the category's structural finding and has no expression here. Composition in this paper is union of element sets between peers; one protocol consuming another as a component is a containment relation the carrier cannot state. The yield category found the same gap one level down, where a curator allocates across protocols.
